  "body": "A rival way of posing the problem: not 'how do we make the flat's agreements stick' but 'what can the asker do, starting now and possibly alone, on the assumption that the agreements may never stick.' The shift matters because every remedy in the selected account — the shared note, the confirmation lines, the review conversation — still draws on the scarcest resource in the flat, which is the avoider's participation and, more generally, all three people's appetite for joint administration. I want a plan that works even if the talks never improve.

The diagnosis I would build on is different too. The chores in this flat live entirely inside a negotiation economy: nothing is owned, nothing is priced, every allocation is temporary and must have its meaning re-established each time. In such a system, disagreeing later about what was agreed is not a malfunction to be engineered away; it is the steady state, because 'what counts as done' and 'what is fair given the rota' are genuinely contestable, and each added definition just produces more text to quarrel over. On this reading, writing agreements down does not remove the friction — it upgrades the litigation. A shared note among friends is also a record, and arguing from a record moves three friends closer to three counterparties. Worse, if the selected account's own unresolved fork is real and the ambiguity is masking a standing fairness grievance, a document can freeze the unfair split in place and hand the wronged person something new to swallow.

So the rival prescription is to shrink the domain that requires agreement, in four moves ordered by how much buy-in they need. First, partition rather than rotate: claim whole domains outright and permanently — I do the kitchen, full stop; the bathroom is yours if you will take it. Ownership dissolves both recurring arguments at once, since 'whose turn' disappears and 'what done means' becomes the owner's standard, with the corollary that non-owners forfeit commentary. The asker can begin this unilaterally: announce a domain, carry it on a fixed cadence regardless of how the talks go, and let visible reliability be the argument. Second, convert what can be converted into money: a cleaner every two or three weeks, split three ways, removes a large fraction of the contested commons in one stroke, and money is the one chore currency adults exchange without imputations about character. Third, where a deal is unavoidable, make it too small to fight about — 'I have the bins this week' rather than a standing arrangement — so that being wrong about it costs days, not months of accumulated grievance. This is the opposite instinct from defining 'done' at greater length: it treats ambiguity as permanent and prices it instead of fighting it.

Fourth, re-read the avoider before approaching them. The selected account reads avoidance as a rational retreat from aversive talks and proposes a one-to-one about making the talks bearable; but that conversation still presupposes the talks are mandatory. A rival reading: the avoidance is a revealed preference for less joint management — the friendship matters to this person, the chore polity does not. The test and the remedy are the same move: offer exits instead of meetings. Take the bins permanently and skip the discussions; or chip in a bit more and we hire help. If they take an exit with relief, the avoidance was never about the tone of the talks — it was about being governed at all. If no exit attracts them either, then the avoidance is about something under the chores, and the honest conversation is 'what do you want this flat to be,' which no chore architecture can pre-script for them.

One thing the original question should not lose: the failure mode here is not a dirty kitchen. It is three friends becoming three litigants. Whatever of this the asker adopts, the friendship needs protecting on purpose — time together that is not flat administration — because the most worrying detail in the description is that the arguments may be the friendship now.

What I cannot resolve: partition needs each person willing to own a domain at a standard the others can live with, and if the avoider owns something and does it badly, the conflict returns as standards-policing, uglier than the turn-taking rows it replaced. The money move assumes slack that may not exist. At those failure points the selected account's conversation-first route stops being a rival and becomes the necessary one.",
  "commitments": "The central claim on offer is that disagreement about what was agreed is the steady state of a fully negotiated chore system, not a drafting failure, so the remedy is reducing what needs agreement rather than improving the agreements. Taking that up means treating it as a conjecture to be tested, not a fact: the flat itself is the test, and if a simple written note actually ended the disputes, that would disconfirm the conjecture locally and weaken the main reason for preferring my route over the selected account's. Attached to that is a criticism of the selected account, which anyone adopting this account would also take on: its documentation centerpiece presumes good-faith ambiguity, and my grounds for doubt are that records among intimates can escalate a quarrel by giving it a text to litigate, that on the account's own unresolved fork a document can entrench an unfair split, and that all its remedies spend the avoider's participation, which is the scarce resource. That criticism is rebuttable — the other account can reply that cheap one-line confirmations depersonalize disagreement precisely because they are cheap — and adopting my account means holding the documentation route in reserve as test and fallback rather than discarding it.

The proposed applications each carry needs: partition needs every flatmate willing to own a domain at a standard the others can tolerate; the money conversion needs budget slack; week-sized deals need tolerance for looser fairness measured over time; the exit offer to the avoider needs the asker to accept an outcome in which one friend barely participates in running the flat, which the asker may experience as a new unfairness borne by themselves. The whole sequence depends further on the asker's capacity to carry an announced share reliably, without reciprocity, for a while; if the asker cannot or will not do that, the unilateral start collapses and the plan defaults to needing the very conversations it was designed to avoid.

Two problems remain open. If an owned domain is done badly, the conflict returns as standards-policing, and my only mechanism against it — non-owners forfeit commentary — may be intolerable in practice. And if the avoidance turns out to be withdrawal from the friendship rather than from the chore polity, no chore architecture is the right instrument, and the 'what do you want this flat to be' conversation is one this account cannot script. What I currently propose to take up is the pose shift — asking what the asker can do alone — plus the four moves as a sequence ordered by buy-in required, with the exit offer doubling as the diagnostic for which reading of the avoider is true.",
}

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
An account of the problem as the material presents it.

Three friends, one flat, recurring arguments about ordinary chores. Two features of the description seem most worth building a conjecture around.

First: agreements are reached, but their content does not survive. They agree who will do something, then later disagree about what the agreement meant. That pattern suggests the agreements are tacit or partial — 'I'll do the kitchen' leaves open how often, until when, and what counts as done — and each party fills in the gaps differently, quite possibly in good faith. When the dispute arrives there is no shared text to appeal to, so the argument reopens as a negotiation about fairness or character, which is harder and more personal. My working conjecture: much of this conflict is an ambiguity-and-memory problem wearing the clothes of a willingness problem.

Second: the conditions keep moving. Changing work schedules mean any fixed split keeps drifting out of date; what seemed fair last month reads as unfair now, prompting renegotiation, which produces further ambiguous agreements. And the friend who now avoids the conversations: avoidance is plausibly a rational response to talks that reliably end in unresolved argument — but it feeds the mechanism, because decisions get made without them, or their silence gets read as consent, seeding the next 'that is not what I agreed to' dispute.

What follows for what to do, with an important limit: the asker is one of three and cannot settle a three-person problem unilaterally. Their realistic moves are proposing, drafting, inviting, and changing their own conduct.

— Replace repeated ad-hoc negotiation with one explicit, small, written arrangement: the recurring chores, who covers each one for now, and for the contested ones a line on what 'done' means and until when. A shared note suffices. The point is not bureaucracy among friends; it is converting 'what did we agree' arguments into checkable facts, and moving friction out of repeated personal confrontation.

— Build in expiry and review. Given schedule churn, time-limit the split ('holds until the rota changes, then we re-split') so changes trigger a planned short conversation instead of silently breaking the deal.

— Stop treating silence as agreement. If the avoider is not in the conversation, do not count them in. And after any agreement, send a one-line confirmation ('bathroom is yours weekly until shifts change — say if that stops working'). This cheaply fixes content while memories are fresh, without any atmosphere of distrust.

— Approach the avoider separately, one-to-one, about the process rather than any particular chore: acknowledge the talks have become aversive, ask what would make them bearable, and offer a concrete minimal proposal — fifteen minutes, a shared note, a monthly revisit — instead of another open-ended 'we need to talk about chores.' This conversation is also diagnostic: their answer will say a lot about whether avoidance is about the arguments or about something deeper.

— Agree less. Some chores can be owned by default or simply left unsystematised; fewer agreements means fewer ambiguous agreements.

One open problem I cannot resolve from the material: whether the disputes really are mostly ambiguity, or whether ambiguity is masking an underlying fairness grievance — one person consistently carrying more. The written-arrangement proposal helps in both cases, but if there is a real imbalance, the review conversation has to surface it explicitly, and that harder conversation may be exactly what the avoider is avoiding. Nothing in the material tells me which situation this is; the conjectures above are structural generalisations, cheap to test and easy to revise if the flat proves them wrong.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
